findings.headline: Forecast £2,902,901 contribution to earmarked reserves in 2026-2027, including business rates held to offset a 2027-2028 income reduction
findings.detail: The report forecasts £2,902,901 of contributions to earmarked reserves. These include additional business rates receipts retained to offset a reduction in income in 2027-2028, extra HRA interest income from the revised internal borrowing adjustment, and budget held for contingency such as Local Government Reorganisation.
findings.matters: Reserves being built to cover a known 2027-2028 business rates income reduction shows forward planning a finance director would want to compare, and the paper names this contribution as the lever if the overspend is not closed.
findings.figures: £2,902,901 forecast contribution to earmarked reserves; General Fund uncommitted reserve balance (17,447) £000s at quarter 2; HRA uncommitted balance (1,603) £000s
findings.quote: Contributions totalling £2,902,901 are forecast to be transferred to Earmarked Reserves in 2026-2027.

findings.headline: Communities and Housing forecasts a £317,000 saving from temporary accommodation income
findings.detail: The paper says the Communities and Housing saving comes from increased income from temporary accommodation, offset by extra staffing costs. It also reports £866,000 of additional grants received, which have matching expenditure in the current year.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation income is a demand-linked revenue stream that other councils dealing with homelessness pressure would want to compare, and it is a case where the paper shows an offsetting gain.
findings.figures: £317,000 Communities and Housing saving (Table 4: (317) £000s); £866,000 additional grants; £125,000 Strategy, Engagement & Culture underspend; £791,000 additional grants
findings.quote: The forecast saving in Communities and Housing of £317,000 is attributable to increased income from the provision of temporary accommodation

findings.headline: HR & Organisational Development forecast £171,000 over budget on agency costs supporting a restructure
findings.detail: The paper attributes the HR & Organisational Development variance to increased agency costs supporting a restructure, plus additional legal expenditure in the year. It says this is mitigated by a saving in Revenues & Benefits from staff vacancies.
findings.matters: Agency costs running alongside a restructure are a common people-cost pressure, and the vacancy offset in Revenues & Benefits shows how the council is covering it.
findings.figures: £171,000 HR & Organisational Development variance; Revenues & Benefits saving of (91) £000s
findings.quote: Additionally, a £171,000 variance in HR & Organisational Development has arisen from increased agency costs supporting a restructure

findings.headline: Climate and Environment forecasts a £688,000 overspend, driven by lower planning fee income
findings.detail: The paper attributes the Climate and Environment overspend mainly to reduced planning fee income, linked to the national and local economy affecting development, and to higher car park operational costs. Planning & Regulatory Services shows the largest single variance within the directorate.
findings.matters: Planning fee income falling with the development cycle is a demand-driven income loss that other councils with similar development pipelines would be tracking.
findings.figures: £688,000 Climate and Environment overspend; £463,000 Planning & Regulatory Services overspend (Table 5: 463 £000s)
findings.quote: which is primarily generated by a reduction in income from planning fees due to the national and local economy impacting development

findings.headline: General Fund capital forecast £1,822,000 underspent, including the Norwich Preservation Trust loan not being made in its current form
findings.detail: The report says the loan to Norwich Preservation Trust is not anticipated to be made in its current form, with a new business case being developed for the site. A removal of the balance from the approved capital programme has been requested. CIL strategic fund contributions are also forecast lower, based on projected developer income.
findings.matters: A capital loan being restructured after a business case rethink is a funding change a lender or finance officer would want to follow, and the CIL shortfall points to developer income assumptions.
findings.figures: £1,822,000 General Fund capital underspend; (1,756) £000s Property and Economic Development variance; (328) £000s CIL strategic fund variance; Norwich Preservation Trust Loan £1,000k removed from budget (Appendix 3: 1,000 to 0)
findings.quote: The loan to Norwich Preservation Trust is not anticipated to be made in its current form and a new business case is being developed

findings.headline: HRA capital programme forecast to be underspent by £14,035,000 in 2026-2027, with £14,035,163 of budget proposed for removal
findings.detail: The paper says the HRA capital programme started later and more slowly than planned, as both new partners onboarded staff and supply chains. Work is now expected to be delivered through quarters 3 and 4, and removal of budgets is proposed. Tower block works await regulator approval before starting.
findings.matters: A £14.0m HRA capital underspend driven by a slow contractor start, with budget removal proposed, is a delivery and borrowing-timing signal a finance director would track against their own capital programme.
findings.figures: £14,035,000 HRA capital underspend; £14,035,163 proposed removal; HRA revised budget £62,758k against forecast outturn £48,723k
findings.quote: the HRA capital programme is projected to be underspent by £14,035,000 for the year.

findings.headline: HRA bad debts provision reduced after an updated assessment, a favourable £521,000 variance
findings.detail: Following an updated assessment, the provision for bad debts has been cut, producing a favourable variance in the HRA forecast.
findings.matters: A release of bad debt provision in the HRA is a change in the council's expected rent arrears exposure, which a lender would read alongside the voids and rent income figures.
findings.figures: £521,000 favourable variance (Table 8: (521) £000s); movement in provision for bad debts to (320) £000s forecast
findings.quote: Following an updated assessment, the provision for bad debts has been reduced, resulting in a favourable variance.

findings.headline: HRA dwelling rents forecast £509,000 above budget on lower voids
findings.detail: The paper attributes the favourable dwelling rent variance to lower than forecast voids levels.
findings.matters: Rent income driven by void performance is a direct lender-relevant revenue indicator for an HRA, and peers can compare void assumptions against their own.
findings.figures: £509,000 favourable dwelling rent variance (Table 8: (509) £000s)
findings.quote: Dwelling rental income is forecast ahead of budget, due to lower than forecast voids levels.

findings.headline: HRA repairs and maintenance forecast £2,265,000 under budget as damp and mould demand falls short of estimate
findings.detail: The paper says reactive and demand-led maintenance expenditure is lower than forecast, partly offset by £2,570,000 of extra pro-active and compliance-based maintenance. It attributes the demand shortfall to the first-year damp and mould estimate, which took account of Awaab's law requirements.
findings.matters: It shows a Awaab's law-driven demand estimate that did not materialise, which other councils budgeting for the same statutory requirement can use as a comparison point.
findings.figures: £2,265,000 reduction in Repairs & Maintenance (Table 8: (2,265) £000s); £2,570,000 increased pro-active and compliance-based maintenance; £305,000 reduction in forecast contributions
findings.quote: The actual level of demand has not met the original forecast.

findings.headline: HRA forecasts a £3,240,000 underspend at quarter 2 2026-2027
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account revenue forecast is an underspend, with the largest favourable variance in Repairs & Maintenance and further favourable variances in bad debts, depreciation and dwelling rents. Some adverse variances, such as Special Services and General Management Property, partly offset these.
findings.matters: A £3.24m HRA underspend at mid-year is a material variance that a finance director would want to understand as either timing, demand, or structural.
findings.figures: £3,240,000 HRA forecast underspend; HRA revenue total (3,240) £000s
findings.quote: which identifies an underspend of £3,240,000.

findings.headline: Norwich forecasts a £697,000 General Fund overspend at quarter 2 2026-2027, with mitigations proposed
findings.detail: The report identifies a forecast General Fund overspend and proposes a budget review, a panel review of overspending budgets, and continued use of the Vacancy Management Panel. If these do not generate enough in-year savings, the report says the pressure could be mitigated by reducing the contribution to earmarked reserves.
findings.matters: It shows a council using a reserves contribution as the fallback lever for a revenue overspend, which a finance director here or at a peer council would want to compare against their own mitigation options.
findings.figures: £697,000 General Fund forecast overspend; Table 1 shows £697k variance; £2,902,901 reserves contribution could be reduced
findings.quote: identifies a forecast overspend of £697,000.

findings.headline: Delivery of affordable housing is affected by high borrowing and construction costs, viability pressures and changes in regulation
findings.detail: The paper reports that 104 new homes were completed across the relevant area in 2026, against 180 in 2025. Enabling works are progressing at Mile Cross and Argyle Street, and the council has approved acquisition of 21 affordable homes at Anglia Square Block C.
findings.matters: The paper names borrowing costs and viability as the constraints on the council's housing pipeline, which bears on the capital and borrowing decisions a lender or peer finance team would track.
findings.figures: 104 new homes completed in 2026; 180 in 2025; 21 affordable homes approved for acquisition at Anglia Square Block C.
findings.quote: affected by high borrowing and construction costs, viability pressures and changes in regulation

findings.headline: Average re-let time for council homes rose from 57 to 68 days against a 21-day target
findings.detail: The paper links the increase to void journey delays and says an end-to-end review of the void process will examine contractor performance, works ordering and repair complexity. Void completions remained around 23 to 25 homes per month.
findings.matters: Longer void periods reduce rental income from HRA stock, and a review of contractor performance is the kind of action a peer council would want to compare.
findings.figures: 68 days (Q2) against a 21-day target; 57 days (Q1).
findings.quote: against a 21-day target

findings.headline: Investment property income fell below its 95% target after one major tenant entered liquidation and its lease was forfeited
findings.detail: The paper attributes the shortfall to a single high-income tenant, and says this does not indicate a wider decline across the portfolio. The property will be marketed for re-letting, with an impact expected in Q3.
findings.matters: A tenant liquidation removing a high-income lease is a concrete commercial income loss, and the re-letting outcome will show whether the council can recover that income.
findings.figures: 95% target; 97% (Q1); Q2 value not stated in the paper.
findings.quote: One major tenant occupying a high-income asset entered liquidation

findings.headline: Business Rates collection recovered to 101.38% against a 100% target after software delays were resolved
findings.detail: The paper says Business Rates collection was 101.38% in Q2, after earlier billing and recovery delays had reduced Q1 performance. Historic cases include outstanding valuation changes.
findings.matters: Collection above 100% of the budget-based target, recovered from a weaker Q1 after a software fix, is a specific income-collection outcome that peer finance teams can compare against.
findings.quote: Collection recovered to 101.38% following the resolution of software delays

findings.headline: The 2027-2028 Financial Strategy is scheduled for consideration in Q3
findings.detail: The Financial Strategy refresh was progressed during Q2 to reflect reducing headroom, ongoing cost pressures and the need for disciplined management of resources. The paper says budget options are to be progressed and that the Council Tax Reduction scheme remains a consideration for budget setting.
findings.matters: The timing of the strategy and the Council Tax Reduction scheme being on the table are the points a lender or peer finance officer would track for the next budget cycle.
findings.figures: None given in the paper.
findings.quote: The strategy is scheduled for consideration in Q3.

findings.headline: An emerging organisational efficiency review is intended to contribute towards the current forecast budget gap
findings.detail: The review will look at non-pay spend, contracts, grants, licences, property costs, income and workforce capacity to identify opportunities to streamline activity and release or redirect capacity. The paper does not quantify the savings or the size of the forecast budget gap.
findings.matters: A finance director would want to know what scale of savings the review is expected to deliver against the forecast gap, and this paper does not yet say.
findings.figures: None given in the paper.
findings.quote: It is intended to contribute towards the current forecast budget gap.

findings.headline: Norwich City Council states it can no longer assume in-year underspends and reserves will provide flexibility, as it prepares its 2027-2028 Financial Strategy
findings.detail: The Investing Wisely scorecard says the council is preparing its 2027-2028 Financial Strategy against reducing financial headroom. It states that in-year underspends and reserves can no longer be relied on to provide flexibility, and that closer scrutiny of expenditure, income and delivery commitments is required.
findings.matters: A council saying it can no longer rely on in-year underspends or reserves signals reduced headroom that a finance director here or at a peer council would need to plan around.
findings.figures: None given in the paper.
findings.quote: The council can no longer assume in-year underspends and reserves will provide flexibility.

findings.paper_title: Anglia Square auditor appointment and business plan update
findings.headline: Cabinet is asked to approve pre-development work on Blocks A and D of Anglia Square, with full plot business plans expected in spring 2027
findings.detail: The paper asks Cabinet to extend existing authority for Block A to cover proportionate pre-development work on both Blocks A and D, which may include a pre-construction services agreement. It states this is not authority to construct, and that full plot business plans and any social or affordable housing funding proposals would come to Cabinet later.
findings.matters: Pre-development spend on two further blocks is being committed before delivery funding and viability are settled, which is a commitment a finance director would want to track against the eventual plot business plans.
findings.figures: Full plot business plans anticipated in spring 2027
findings.quote: Cabinet is therefore requested to approve the extension of the existing authority for Block A to enable the Investment Partnership, where agreed between the Council and Aviva Capital Partners, to undertake proportionate pre-development work for both Blocks A and D.

findings.paper_title: Anglia Square auditor appointment and business plan update
findings.headline: Anglia Square investment partnership business plan runs to March 2027, with next overarching plan due before end of March 2027 for April 2027 to March 2028
findings.detail: The paper says the current investment partnership business plan is predicated on the HIF grant and runs to March 2027, while the grant period is now expected to extend further. Officers recommend confirming the existing plan rather than resubmitting it, with the next plan to cover April 2027 to March 2028.
findings.matters: The governing budget for a joint venture with council investment lapses before the grant it depends on is expected to finish, which a finance officer elsewhere would want to see in a similar JV.
findings.figures: Current business plan currency to end of March 2027; next plan covers April 2027 to end of March 2028
findings.quote: The next overarching business plan will therefore be produced before the end of March 2027 and will cover a period from April 2027 to the end of March 2028.

findings.paper_title: Anglia Square auditor appointment and business plan update
findings.headline: Council is seeking to extend the Homes England HIF grant defrayment period from the end of March 2027 into 2028, after asbestos and archaeology delays on the Anglia Square main site
findings.detail: The paper says the programme for the grant-funded expenditure has been delayed, first by additional asbestos removal and now by the archaeology programme, which could run into 2028. It states that the total HIF grant sum is still not expected to be exceeded, but that the expenditure profile will now extend into 2028.
findings.matters: A grant-funded regeneration scheme is seeking a later spend deadline from Homes England, and a finance director or lender would want to know whether the grant position and the council's exposure change as a result.
findings.figures: HIF defrayment period currently to the end of March 2027; extension sought into 2028
findings.quote: An extension is therefore being sought to extend the period for defraying the HIF grant into 2028.

findings.headline: The paper says Norwich has operated without a formal agency recruitment framework since 2016, with agency engagements on varying terms and charge rates.
findings.detail: The paper describes temporary recruitment as managed through individual agency engagements with different contractual terms, charge rates and levels of oversight. It says this limits visibility of agency expenditure. The paper gives no current agency spend total as a baseline for the framework's spend KPIs.
findings.matters: Councils without a corporate agency arrangement, and lenders assessing workforce cost control, can compare how this council is moving to a framework with its own spend data.
findings.figures: Previous arrangements expired in 2016; no agency spend figure given
findings.quote: The Council has operated without a formal agency recruitment framework

findings.headline: The paper states there are no specific budgetary implications from procuring the multi-supplier agency framework.
findings.detail: The financial section says the framework itself carries no budget implications and expects improved value for money and spend visibility. It also says current arrangements limit the council's ability to negotiate rates and control costs.
findings.matters: A council entering a framework with no stated budget cost, while agency spend is not quantified in the paper, is a position a finance director elsewhere may want to compare with their own procurement business cases.
findings.figures: none stated
findings.quote: There are no specific budgetary implications as a result of procuring a multi

findings.headline: Norwich's HR team has reduced a temporary-to-permanent conversion fee from 35% to 20%, according to the paper.
findings.detail: The paper cites recent HR negotiations that cut the fee charged when a temporary worker is converted to permanent employment. It presents this as evidence of the savings available through stronger contract management.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can benchmark this conversion fee against the terms in its own agency contracts.
findings.figures: Conversion fee reduced from 35% to 20%
findings.quote: temporary-to-permanent conversion fee from 35% to 20%, demonstrating

findings.headline: The Bank of England interest base rate stands at 3.75%, with rate reductions now seen as less likely
findings.detail: The paper gives the current Bank Rate and says the likelihood of rate reductions has reduced significantly, particularly if inflationary pressure feeds into consumer pricing. It also notes that commentators expect upward pressure from energy prices, and that CPI inflation for the year to September 2026 is well below the 2022-23 peaks.
findings.matters: The council's borrowing and investment costs track Bank Rate, and a finance director, or a lender pricing new funding, will want to see how the council's own risk register reads the rate outlook.
findings.figures: 3.75%; CPI inflation for the year to September 2026
findings.quote: The Bank of England interest base rate currently stands at 3.75%

findings.headline: CORP06 business continuity risk score is 'worsening' in quarter two following an August 2026 internal audit
findings.detail: The paper says the quarter two score for CORP06 is worsening because of an internal audit outcome in August 2026, and because a number of actions must be implemented in quarter three. It also cites an elevation in UK Government preparedness guidance for the coming winter period. The risk is reported as outside the council's risk appetite for both current and target scores.
findings.matters: An internal audit finding that moves a corporate risk score the wrong way, with actions due in the next quarter, is a control weakness other finance and governance officers can check their own arrangements against.
findings.figures: internal audit in August 2026; actions due in quarter three
findings.quote: the quarter two risk score is worsening following review due to the outcome of an internal audit in August 2026

findings.headline: CORP09 Anglia Square risk impact reduced in quarter two as financial risk falls with site works
findings.detail: The paper reports that CORP09 was reviewed in Q2 and its risk impact has come down. The reason given is that the quantum of financial risk is falling as the council progresses with the site works.
findings.matters: A large regeneration scheme whose financial exposure is shrinking as works progress is a capital position a finance director, or a lender assessing the council's contingent liabilities, would want to track.
findings.figures: no figures given in the paper
findings.quote: the risk impact has reduced as the as the quantum of financial risk is falling as the council progresses with the site works.

findings.headline: Norwich has received a provisional three-year financial settlement, effective from April 2026
findings.detail: The paper says the reforms to local government finance gave the council a provisional three-year settlement from April 2026. The council states this gives greater funding certainty for its medium-term financial planning. Preparation of the 2027-28 budget is described as progressing.
findings.matters: A multi-year settlement gives a finance director a longer funding horizon to plan against, and peers will want to compare how far their own settlements cover the same period.
findings.figures: three-year provisional settlement; effective from April 2026
findings.quote: the council has received a provisional three-year financial settlement, effective from April 2026. This provides greater funding certainty

findings.headline: The council reports there is still some reliance on interim and agency staff in certain roles, which the Vacancy Management Panel is overseeing
findings.detail: The paper says the Vacancy Management Panel and workforce plan are intended to sustain capability and reduce temporary staffing cost. It states that reliance on interim and agency cover continues in certain roles during the period of uncertainty around Local Government Reorganisation.
findings.matters: Temporary staffing cost is a recurring budget pressure, and a council under reorganisation uncertainty is a case other finance directors may compare with their own agency spend.
findings.figures: none stated
findings.quote: there is still some reliance on Interim/agency use to cover certain roles

findings.headline: The council has set up an investment partnership with Aviva Capital Partners to progress delivery of Anglia Square
findings.detail: The paper says the council purchased the Anglia Square site in 2024-25 with Homes England grant funding and has worked with Homes England on due diligence. It says the partnership's business plan is approved by Cabinet and overseen through the shareholder panel.
findings.matters: A council-led regeneration partnership with a private investor, supported by grant, is a structure other councils and lenders to councils will compare with their own developments.
findings.figures: none stated
findings.quote: The council has also set up an investment partnership with Aviva Capital Partners to progress delivery of Anglia Square.

findings.headline: The Regulator of Social Housing awarded the council a C1 rating following its January 2026 inspection
findings.detail: The paper reports that the council's housing management and governance were assessed in January 2026 and given a C1 rating, which it describes as the highest score a housing provider can achieve. It states that at the time Norwich was one of nine councils to achieve this rating.
findings.matters: A top regulatory rating for the housing service, and the paper's count of nine councils with the same rating, give peers a benchmark for their own housing governance.
findings.figures: C1 rating; one of nine councils with this rating at the time
findings.quote: Following the inspection NCC were awarded a C1 rating, this being the highest score a housing provider can achieve

findings.headline: The October 2025 external audit of Local Government Transparency Code compliance gave a limited assurance opinion with 8 recommendations
findings.detail: The audit made 8 recommendations, 3 urgent, 4 important and 1 routine. The paper says 3 of the recommendations remain open as important, and they are tracked through the audit tracker.
findings.matters: Transparency Code compliance is a published, comparable test of council data disclosure, and a limited assurance opinion on it is a finding other finance officers can benchmark.
findings.figures: 8 recommendations (3 urgent, 4 important, 1 routine); 3 still open as important
findings.quote: The audit made 8 recommendations: 3 as urgent, 4 as important and 1 as routine. Currently 3 of the recommendations remain as important.

findings.headline: Lion Homes (Norwich) Ltd is in a Members' Voluntary Liquidation, with the process due to conclude in June 2026
findings.detail: The paper records Limited Assurance for Lion Homes in 2024-25 and a 2025 decision to place the company into a Members' Voluntary Liquidation. A temporary Company Secretary has been appointed to oversee the liquidation and support the council's other companies.
findings.matters: A wholly owned council company in liquidation, with delayed accounts, is a governance and balance sheet exposure that finance directors and lenders with council group exposure will want to track.
findings.figures: MVL process to conclude June 2026
findings.quote: A temporary Company Secretary has been appointed to oversee the Members’ Voluntary Liquidation of Lion Homes and to provide additional capacity to support the Council’s other companies.

findings.headline: The 2024/25 Statement of Accounts and audit were completed in March 2026, with the 2025/26 audit underway to November 2026
findings.detail: The paper says the council is returning to timely annual audits under the statutory backstop timetable, after a national backlog. The 2024/25 results report identified several improvements to company governance and financial reporting.
findings.matters: A council returning to the audit timetable after the backlog is following the same backstop dates that other councils must meet, so its progress is directly comparable.
findings.figures: 2025/26 audit underway to November 2026
findings.quote: The 2024/25 Statement of Accounts and audit were completed in March 2026.

findings.headline: EY's Audit Results Report on the 2024/25 accounts included two Value for Money risks of significant weaknesses
findings.detail: The two risks cover governance of solely owned subsidiary companies and timely financial reporting. The council's responses to each are set out in the paper.
findings.matters: Significant weaknesses in value for money arrangements are a formal external audit finding, and the two areas named (subsidiary governance and closedown timing) are common pressure points at other councils.
findings.figures: two Value for Money risks of significant weaknesses
findings.quote: EY’s Audit Results Report (ARR) included two Value for Money risks of significant weaknesses

findings.headline: The council set a balanced 2026/27 budget without drawing on reserves
findings.detail: The paper states that the council was able to set a balanced budget for 2026/27 without drawing down from reserves. It sits within a section on the Medium-Term Financial Strategy.
findings.matters: A balanced budget with no reserve drawdown is a specific position a finance director can test against their own 2026/27 plan and reserve strategy.
findings.figures: none stated
findings.quote: For 2026/27 the council was able to set a balanced budget without the need to drawdown from reserves.

findings.headline: The provisional 2025-26 capital programme was underspent by £22.255m on the General Fund and £16.036m on the HRA
findings.detail: The paper gives the provisional capital outturn for 2025-26 as an underspend against both the General Fund and HRA programmes. It links to the provisional outturn report to Cabinet.
findings.matters: Two large capital underspends in one year are a delivery and phasing signal that finance officers at other councils will want to compare against their own programmes.
findings.figures: £22.255m General Fund capital underspend; £16.036m HRA capital underspend
findings.quote: Additionally, the capital provisional outturn was a £22.255m underspend against the General Fund and £16.036m underspend against the HRA programmes.

findings.headline: The provisional 2025-26 General Fund revenue outturn was a £0.543m underspend, which the paper says contributed to reserves
findings.detail: The paper reports a provisional General Fund revenue underspend of £0.543m for 2025-26, which it says was added to reserves. It also reports a Housing Revenue Account surplus of £4.391m, to be used in future budget planning.
findings.matters: A finance director comparing 2025-26 outturn and reserve movements can read the General Fund and HRA positions side by side, and the HRA surplus is earmarked for future budget planning.
findings.figures: £0.543m General Fund underspend; £4.391m HRA surplus
findings.quote: The provisional outturn for 2025-26 was a £0.543m underspend on the General Fund revenue Account (subsequently contributing to reserves) and a surplus of £4.391m on the Housing Revenue Account (HRA) which will be utilised in future budget planning.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Norwich City Council, Audit Results Report Year ended 31 March 2026

findings.detail: The auditor rates timeliness of the draft financial statements as 'Effective'. It also records working papers were delivered to the agreed timetable and the finance team was accessible throughout the audit.
findings.matters: Meeting the 30 June deadline is a measure other councils track against their own closedown timetables.
findings.figures: 30 June 2026 deadline
findings.quote: The financial statements were published by the 30 June 2026 deadline set out in the Accounts and Audit Regulations.

findings.headline: The auditor identified several misstatements in the draft financial statements, comprising five adjustments to the primary statements and six to disclosure notes.
findings.detail: The auditor rates the volume and value of misstatements as 'Requires improvement', while the volume of disclosure misstatements is rated 'Effective'. The report says the draft statements were otherwise of good quality and were published by the statutory deadline.
findings.matters: Finance teams at other councils can compare their own statement-preparation quality against the auditor's rating, which is part of the factors affecting audit execution.
findings.figures: 5 adjustments to primary financial statements; 6 adjustments to disclosure notes
findings.quote: We identified five adjustments to the primary financial statements and six adjustments to disclosure notes.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Norwich City Council, Audit Results Report Year ended 31 March 2026
findings.headline: The Council's valuer's one investment property valuation of £8.87 million was found outside the auditor's range, creating a judgemental audit difference of £1.08 million.
findings.detail: The auditor's valuation specialists found one property valuation above their reasonable range of £7.24 million to £7.79 million, mainly because of the yield used. Four of five sampled valuations were within range. The specialists also noted the valuer's adjustments of 2% for acquisition and disposal costs were not consistent with conventional UK practice.
findings.matters: The same 2% cost adjustment and gross-yield approach would affect other councils' property valuations, so peers will want to check their own valuer's methodology.
findings.figures: £8.87 million valuation; £7.24 million to £7.79 million reasonable range; £1.08 million judgemental audit difference
findings.quote: This resulted in a judgemental audit difference of £1.08 million.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Norwich City Council, Audit Results Report Year ended 31 March 2026
findings.headline: The auditor records that Lion Homes Limited's refinancing would have needed to be provided at significantly higher interest rates under subsidy control requirements.
findings.detail: The report says the Council considered refinancing the company's existing borrowing and providing additional financial support. Advice it obtained indicated that refinancing would need significantly higher rates to comply with subsidy control, and the auditor's review cites this alongside adverse market conditions and the company's financial position.
findings.matters: Subsidy control limits on refinancing a council-owned company's debt affect how other councils and lenders assess exposure to council subsidiaries.
findings.quote: advice obtained by the Council indicated that any refinancing would need to be provided at significantly higher interest rates to comply with subsidy control requirements.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Norwich City Council, Audit Results Report Year ended 31 March 2026
findings.headline: The auditor reports a significant weakness in the Council's governance of Lion Homes Limited for 2025/26, having been unable to confirm that the 2024/25 actions were complete.
findings.detail: The report says the 2024/25 significant weakness in oversight of subsidiary entities remained for 2025/26. It notes progress on whistleblowing arrangements but says the constitutional amendments and lessons learned review were not finalised by 31 March 2026. The auditor also records that the Council resolved to pursue liquidation of Lion Homes.
findings.matters: Other councils with arm's-length companies will see how an auditor applies a significant-weakness finding to subsidiary oversight, and lenders will see a documented control gap at the Council.
findings.quote: The significant weakness therefore remained for 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Norwich City Council, Audit Results Report Year ended 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Auditor expects to issue a disclaimed opinion on the Council's 2025/26 financial statements, with an unqualified opinion anticipated by 2028/29.
findings.detail: The auditor reports that it has substantially completed the audit and expects a disclaimed opinion, subject to outstanding procedures. The report says progress has been made in rebuilding assurance after the 2023/24 disclaimed opinion, and limitations remain for reserves, historical PP&E and Investment Properties.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council, or a lender, needs to know how far the audit trail has been rebuilt and when a clean opinion is expected.
findings.figures: Unqualified opinion anticipated by 2028/29; 2025/26 opinion disclaimed
findings.quote: we expect to issue a disclaimed opinion.

findings.headline: New CORP38E risk replaces four Local Government Reorganisation risks, covering uncertainty during the pause
findings.detail: CORP38E replaces the four LGR risks previously on the register. It captures risks arising from uncertainty about LGR and from balancing business as usual against preparation for any new unitary authority. The paper also says there are no material LGR implications for this report.
findings.matters: Councils facing reorganisation, and their lenders and finance teams, need to know how the risk of balancing business as usual against unitary preparation is being recorded and managed.
findings.figures: four LGR risks replaced by one (CORP38E)
findings.quote: This risk has replaced the four Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) risk that were previously included on the risk register.

findings.headline: Bank of England base rate stands at 3.75%, and the paper says the likelihood of rate reductions has reduced significantly
findings.detail: The paper gives the current Bank of England base rate and says that, due to recent global events, the prospect of rate reductions has fallen significantly, especially if inflationary pressure feeds into consumer prices. It also notes that CPI is above the 2% target, though well below the 2022-23 peaks.
findings.matters: The base rate and the expected rate path feed directly into the cost of PWLB and other borrowing, which affects the council's borrowing plans and its lenders' assessment of its position.
findings.figures: 3.75% Bank of England base rate; CPI above 2% target
findings.quote: The Bank of England interest base rate currently stands at 3.75%, due to recent global events, the likelihood of rate of reductions has reduced significantly

findings.headline: Council receives a provisional three-year financial settlement effective from April 2026
findings.detail: The paper says reforms to local government finance have given the council a provisional three-year settlement from April 2026. It says this gives greater funding certainty for medium-term financial planning.
findings.matters: Multi-year settlement certainty changes how finance directors and lenders assess medium-term income, and the council is preparing its 2027-28 budget on this basis.
findings.figures: three-year settlement, effective from April 2026
findings.quote: the council has received a provisional three-year financial settlement, effective from April 2026.

findings.headline: Higher-risk building fire risk impact raised to possible fatality or life-changing injury and escalated to the corporate register
findings.detail: CORP39 moved up from the Communities and Housing Directorate register. The likelihood is unchanged because the fabric of the buildings has not materially changed, but the impact score has increased. The paper says condition inspections and surveys are continuing for each affected building.
findings.matters: A corporate risk escalation to fatality-level impact on higher-risk buildings is a liability and remediation exposure that finance officers and lenders would want to track, though the paper gives no cost figures.
findings.quote: the assessed risk impact has increased to reflect the possibility of a fire in a higher risk building resulting in a fatality or life-changing injury.

findings.headline: Anglia Square financial risk impact reduced at Q2 as site works progress
findings.detail: CORP09 was reviewed in Q2 and its risk impact was reduced. The paper says the quantum of financial risk is falling as the council progresses with the site works.
findings.matters: A reduction in the financial exposure on a major regeneration site is a change a finance director and lenders would track against the scheme's capital position.
findings.quote: the risk impact has reduced as the as the quantum of financial risk is falling as the council progresses with the site works.

findings.headline: Business continuity risk score rises at Q2 following an August 2026 internal audit and winter preparedness guidance
findings.detail: The Q2 review raised the score for CORP06, the failure to respond to a critical business continuity event. The paper links the change to an internal audit outcome in August 2026 and to actions due in quarter three, and it also cites the government's elevated winter preparedness guidance.
findings.matters: A finance director would want to know that an internal audit has moved a corporate risk score, and that the related actions fall due in the next quarter.
findings.quote: the quarter two risk score is worsening following review due to the outcome of an internal audit in August 2026

findings.headline: Six community centres will be fast-tracked for solar PV in 2026/27, with a £200k budget confirmed by the capital board.
findings.detail: The paper says feasibility studies for decarbonised heating and solar PV are complete for all operational General Fund assets, and financing options are being researched. It records that the council's capital board has confirmed the £200k budget for the six community centres.
findings.matters: A confirmed capital budget for a decarbonisation programme, with financing options still being researched, shows how a council is moving from feasibility studies to funded delivery.
findings.figures: £200k budget; six community centres
findings.quote: with £200k budget confirmed by the

findings.headline: Business continuity risk CORP06 records a TIAA audit outcome of limited assurance, with actions to address it.
findings.detail: The paper states that the audit outcome meeting was held on 11 August and that the head of service agreed a timetable for completing the actions. It notes that out-of-hours cover gaps have again been highlighted in the TIAA audit.
findings.matters: A limited assurance opinion on business continuity, with out-of-hours cover still open, is an audit weakness that peer councils and lenders would weigh against operational resilience.
findings.quote: Actions to address audit outcome - limited assurance

findings.headline: Anglia Square: discussions with Homes England have raised a possible extension of time and a deed of variation to the grant agreement.
findings.detail: The paper records a positive discussion with Homes England on the potential risk, including the possibility of an extension of time and a deed of variation to the grant agreement. The matter is to be raised higher within Homes England.
findings.matters: Changes to grant timing or terms on a £34 million scheme affect the council's funding profile and exposure, which a finance officer or lender would track.
findings.figures: £34 million Homes England grant
findings.quote: the possibility of an extension of time and deed of variation to the grant agreement

findings.headline: Anglia Square: the remaining Homes England grant is now under £10m, and demolition spend is higher than anticipated.
findings.detail: The paper says demolition spend is higher than anticipated but is being managed with contingencies and underspends on archaeology and utilities. It says the impact of this will reduce as works progress and the outstanding grant to be spent reduces.
findings.matters: A finance director, here or elsewhere, would want to know how a grant-funded regeneration scheme is absorbing cost pressure and how much grant is left to draw.
findings.figures: £34 million Homes England grant; remaining grant under £10m
findings.quote: remaining grant is now under £10m.

findings.headline: Norwich's Head of Property & Economic Development states the commercial property portfolio is being managed "effectively, prudently" and in line with strategic objectives
findings.detail: The response to a Member's query on the commercial property portfolio cites Asset & Development Board and Capital Board oversight, regular financial monitoring and an ongoing asset review programme. It states that independent internal and external audit reviews have provided assurance, and the action is marked Completed.
findings.matters: Commercial property exposure is a common concern for councils and lenders, and this is the council's own assurance statement on how the portfolio is run, with no figures given.
findings.quote: The Council’s commercial property portfolio is being managed effectively, prudently and in line with strategic objectives.

findings.headline: Cabinet agreed to keep the climate change risk (CORP21) on Norwich's Corporate Risk Register, after the Audit Committee asked for it to be reconsidered
findings.detail: The Audit Committee asked Cabinet to reconsider de-escalating CORP21 Climate Change Risk from the Corporate Risk Register. The item was shared with Cabinet on 10 June 2026, and the action is marked Completed.
findings.matters: A council's decision to keep or drop a named risk from its corporate register shows how its committee and Cabinet handle risk escalation, which peers and lenders may compare.
findings.quote: Cabinet discussed the deescalation and agreed to keep it on the Corporate Risk Register.

findings.headline: Norwich's housing property data is primarily input manually into the NEC database, and a proposal to capture it through the NEC surveying tool is put forward
findings.detail: The Director of Property (Housing) response says NEC is the primary property database and that investment planning and decisions are driven from it. The response identifies manual input as creating inefficiencies and human-error risk, and proposes on-site capture synchronised to NEC; the item is marked Outstanding with a due date of 10/11/2026.
findings.matters: Investment planning for a council housing stock rests on this data, so a stated data-quality weakness and its proposed fix bear on how far the stock's condition figures can be relied on.
findings.quote: Currently the updates to the database are primarily input manually creating inefficiencies and increasing the risk of human error.

findings.headline: Norwich's Transparency and Information audit received a "limited assurance" opinion, and the report on the response is due at a future Audit Committee meeting
findings.detail: The Regulator of Social Housing item asks the Head of Legal and Governance to report on actions taken after the limited assurance opinion. The action is marked In Progress and has been added to the work programme as TBC, with a due date of 07/05/2027.
findings.matters: A limited assurance opinion from a regulator-linked audit on transparency and information is an audit weakness a lender or peer finance team would want to track to closure.
findings.quote: To ask the Head of Legal and Governance to present a report to a future meeting of the Audit Committee on the actions taken to respond to the limited assurance opinion on the Transparency and Information audit.

findings.paper_title: Procurement of Temporary Accommodation for Homeless Households
findings.headline: No alternative options available to meet statutory homelessness duty
findings.detail: Council has legal duty under Part VII Housing Act 1996 to secure suitable interim accommodation for eligible homeless applicants while applications are assessed (up to 56 days). The paper confirms that to comply with legislation, there are no other viable options available to the council.
findings.matters: Finance directors assess mandatory versus discretionary spending; this confirms homelessness accommodation is a non-negotiable budget item regardless of cost pressures or market conditions.
findings.figures: Assessment period up to 56 days
findings.quote: To comply with legislation there are no other viable options.

findings.paper_title: Procurement of Temporary Accommodation for Homeless Households
findings.headline: Rising demand and increasing accommodation costs identified as financial risk to council budgets
findings.detail: Financial risk management section identifies that rising demand and increasing accommodation costs may place additional pressure on council budgets. The paper notes that market conditions may result in higher contract costs than anticipated. The actual contract value is not disclosed in the public paper.
findings.matters: Finance directors watch budget pressures in services they cannot reduce; homelessness accommodation is a statutory obligation, meaning cost increases must be absorbed and cannot be deferred or avoided.
findings.figures: Contract value detailed in exempt appendix only
findings.quote: Rising demand and increasing accommodation costs may place additional pressure on Council budgets... market conditions may result in higher contract costs than anticipated.

findings.paper_title: Procurement of Temporary Accommodation for Homeless Households
findings.headline: Contract for 38 units of temporary accommodation expiring November 2026 requires procurement exercise
findings.detail: Council currently operates 60 units of procured temporary accommodation. The contract for 38 of these units expires in November 2026. Procurement will seek to secure a minimum of 38 units over a three-year contract period with option to extend for two further years. This addresses statutory duty to provide interim accommodation under the Housing Act 1996.
findings.matters: Finance directors monitor service continuity and budget planning; expiring contracts create timing pressure to rebid services during uncertain market conditions, with statutory obligations meaning costs cannot be avoided.
findings.figures: 60 units currently; 38 units expiring; 38 units minimum sought over three years
findings.quote: The Council currently has 60 units of procured temporary accommodation for homeless households with the contract for 38 of these units due to expire in November 2026.

findings.headline: Council repaid £53.2m of debt in 2025-26 with no new borrowing, while maintaining £68.5m cash reserves
findings.detail: The council repaid £53.2m of PWLB debt during the year and took zero new external borrowing. In July 2025 it early-repaid a £5m Barclays market loan and received a £554k discount from the lender. Officers are deferring any new borrowing pending lower interest rates, despite a capital financing requirement of £314m and maturing debt of £7.5m due in 2026-27.
findings.matters: The council's ability to repay significant debt demonstrates financial strength, but the absence of new borrowing despite an unfinanced borrowing need of £168m suggests the council is relying on reserve drawdown or deferring refinancing—both relevant to a lender's assessment of future refinancing needs and cash sustainability.
findings.figures: £53.200m PWLB repaid, zero new borrowing, £554k discount on early repayment, £68.453m cash reserves, £314.061m CFR
findings.quote: The Council opted to re-pay its Barclays £5m loan early, in July 2025. In June, the Council's Treasury Advisors (MUFG) advised market conditions are such that the lender would pay the council a discount for early redemption of the loan (circa £554K).

findings.headline: Capital programme spent only 60% of budget, £38.3m underspent
findings.detail: The council spent £56.5m of a £94.8m capital budget, a shortfall of £38.3m (40%). General Fund capital was £23m underspent and HRA capital £16m underspent. This reduction also lowered the year's borrowing requirement to £4.7m versus the budgeted £7.5m.
findings.matters: Persistent major capital underspending raises questions about the council's ability to deliver planned investment programmes, maintain assets at expected standards, and execute approved capital strategies.
findings.figures: £56.477m actual, £94.768m budget, £38.291m underspent
findings.quote: Actual capital spending was under budget for the year by £38.291m.

findings.headline: General Fund financing costs 7.54% of net revenue against 0.97% forecast, mainly due to unbudgeted IFRS 16 impacts and Minimum Revenue Provision changes
findings.detail: The council estimated general fund financing costs at 0.97% of net revenue but the actual outturn was 7.54%. The paper attributes this to unbudgeted impacts of IFRS 16 implementation (requiring leases to be capitalized on the balance sheet) and unexpected changes to Minimum Revenue Provision policy, described as unknown when the treasury strategy was prepared. This follows a similar pattern in 2024-25 (0.29% estimate versus 5.22% actual).
findings.matters: A 750-basis-point miss in forecasting debt service affordability signals forecasting weaknesses and suggests the council may not fully understand the ongoing costs of major accounting changes. A lender needs assurance that the council can accurately predict and sustain its debt service burden.
findings.figures: 0.97% budgeted, 7.54% actual for 2025-26; prior year 0.29% budgeted versus 5.22% actual
findings.quote: The table below shows that the general fund outturn is higher than the estimate mainly due to the unbudgeted changes following the implementation of IFRS16 in 2024-25 (impact unknown when the TMS was prepared) and the unbudgeted changes to minimum revenue provision

findings.headline: Council subsidiary Lion Homes failed to repay £6.15m of loans due and is being liquidated
findings.detail: Lion Homes (Norwich) Ltd, a private company wholly owned by the council, did not repay loans of £6.15m that were due on 31 March 2025. No new loans were made in 2025-26. On 9 July 2025, Cabinet approved a Members Voluntary Liquidation of the company, which is expected to complete in 2026-27.
findings.matters: A material council-owned subsidiary cannot service its debt, representing a significant asset loss to the council and raising questions about group governance and oversight of trading companies.
findings.figures: £6.150m due and unpaid, voluntary liquidation underway
findings.quote: During 2025-2026 LHL did not repay any of its loans which were due to be repaid on 31st March 2025. No new loans were made to LHL during 2025-26 and the total amount due to be repaid was £6.150m. On 9th July 2025 Cabinet approved the recommendation received from the Lion Homes Shareholder Panel to undertake a Members Voluntary Liquidation of the company.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Audit Committee Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Norwich missed the statutory deadline for publishing its 2024/25 accounts, raising questions about financial reporting capability.
findings.detail: The council did not meet the 27 February 2026 deadline for public publication of the 2024/25 Accounts — the publication was delayed. The Committee specifically sought assurance that this delay did not reflect underlying financial resilience issues. The council has since confirmed it will meet future deadlines and has committed to improving timeliness.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director views timely, accurate accounts publication as fundamental to financial governance. Missing a statutory deadline indicates process or resource problems and prompts questions about the council's financial health and control environment.
findings.figures: 27 February 2026 (statutory deadline missed)
findings.quote: The Council did not meet the statutory audit backlog date of 27 February 2026 for the public publication of the Accounts

findings.paper_title: Adjustments to the Capital Programme - Rose Lane MSCP equipment upgrades
findings.headline: Rose Lane MSCP generates approximately £899,000 annually to the General Fund; equipment installed in 2016 has reached end of serviceable life and council proposes £95,000 replacement
findings.detail: The parking management equipment and CCTV systems installed in 2016 have reached the end of their operational life, creating increasing risks of equipment failure, service disruption and lost income. The council is seeking capital approval for £95,000 equipment replacement, to be funded from available General Fund capital receipts, ensuring continued operation of this significant revenue-generating asset.
findings.matters: A lender would want to know whether a council's material revenue-generating assets are being maintained adequately and whether the council has spare capital receipts to fund necessary capital investment
findings.figures: approximately £899,000 to the General Fund during the 2025/26 financial year; £95,000 capital investment
findings.quote: The car park also generates a significant and reliable income stream for the Council, contributing approximately £899,000 to the General Fund during the 2025/26 financial year.

findings.headline: Property, Plant and Equipment (£1,075 million) and Investment Property (£96 million) can only receive partial assurance; material assets remain unaudited due to valuation cycle disruption from 2021/22 disclaimer
findings.detail: Major balance sheet assets totalling £1.17 billion cannot receive substantial audit assurance. The auditors note that due to the valuation cycle, many assets have not been subject to revaluation or audit procedures since the 2021/22 disclaimer. The auditors state the maximum assurance achievable is partial.
findings.matters: These are the council's largest asset classes; partial audit assurance on £1.17bn of assets indicates unresolved valuation issues and limits lender confidence in the balance sheet.
findings.figures: PPE net book value £1,075.25 million; Investment Property £96.20 million
findings.quote: The maximum assurance level we will be able to report in 2025/26 will be partial, as due to the valuations cycle in place at the Council, there are a number of assets that have not been subject to revaluation in the period that, following previous disclaimers of opinion, have not been subject to audit procedures.

findings.headline: Auditors unable to obtain substantial assurance over council reserves, with only partial assurance expected, persisting from 2021/22 disclaimer of opinion
findings.detail: The auditors explicitly state they cannot provide substantial assurance over the council's useable and unusable reserves pending completion of work to rebuild assurance following a disclaimer issued in 2021/22—three years ago. Reserves are expected to receive only Partial assurance in 2025/26.
findings.matters: Reserves are the council's financial shock absorber and directly affect its resilience and borrowing capacity; inability to audit them properly after three years represents a material audit limitation and suggests unresolved governance issues.
findings.figures: Expected assurance rating 2025/26: Partial (vs Substantial for most other account areas)
findings.quote: Until we have completed our work programme on the rebuilding of assurance following the disclaimed audit opinions, we are unable to obtain substantial assurance over the useable and unusable reserves of the Council reported in the financial statements.

findings.headline: Subsidiary Lion Homes undergoing liquidation with unaudited 2023/24 and missing 2024/25 financial statements, consolidated on break-up basis
findings.detail: Lion Homes (Norwich) Ltd is in Members' Voluntary Liquidation. Its 2023/24 financial statements have not been audited and filed. No 2024/25 financial statements have been prepared. The company has been consolidated into group accounts on a break-up basis rather than a going-concern basis, which auditors could not fully assure.
findings.matters: A subsidiary in liquidation with unaudited financial statements creates material uncertainty in group borrowing capacity and financial position; group accounts can only receive partial assurance because auditors cannot verify subsidiary valuations.
findings.figures: Auditors can only provide Partial expected assurance rating for Group financial statements and consolidation
findings.quote: Lion Homes (Norwich) Ltd is currently undergoing a Members' Voluntary Liquidation process. The Company's financial statements for 2023/24 have not been audited and filed. The 2024/25 financial statements have not yet been prepared. As a result, no subsidiary auditor reporting was prepared for 2024/25. The company has therefore been consolidated into the Group financial statements on a break-up basis.

findings.paper_title: Supplementary Agenda Document Pack - Audit committee - 15/09/2026
findings.headline: Group financial statements consolidation work incomplete; expected only Partial assurance in 2025/26
findings.detail: EY issued no assurance on group financial statements in 2024/25 and expects only Partial assurance in 2025/26. Work remains dependent on receiving component auditors' reporting deliverables within agreed timescales. The auditors' ability to conclude depends on subsidiary and related-entity audit work being completed.

findings.figures: Group financial statements: None (2023/24), None (2024/25), Partial expected (2025/26)
findings.quote: We are currently completing our testing in this area and expect to obtain assurance over the closing balance as at 31 March 2026, subject to the satisfactory completion of our remaining audit procedures and review processes. This is dependent on receiving the component auditor's reporting deliverables in accordance with the agreed timetable.

findings.paper_title: Supplementary Agenda Document Pack - Audit committee - 15/09/2026
findings.headline: Reserves cannot be fully assured; auditors rebuilding assurance following disclaimed audit opinion
findings.detail: The Council's useable and unusable reserves cannot be given substantial assurance in 2025/26 because the auditors are still on a programme to rebuild assurance following the disclaimed opinion. Reserves remain at 'Partial' assurance level in the current year.
findings.matters: Reserves are a key metric of financial resilience for local government finance. Inability to audit them reliably creates uncertainty about the true financial position available to meet future pressures or fund services.
findings.figures: Reserves: expected 'Partial' assurance in 2025/26; no assurance in 2023/24 or 2024/25; assurance rebuild following disclaimed opinion
findings.quote: Until we have completed our work programme on the rebuilding of assurance following the disclaimed audit opinions, we are unable to obtain substantial assurance over the useable and unusable reserves of the Council reported in the financial statements.

findings.paper_title: Supplementary Agenda Document Pack - Audit committee - 15/09/2026
findings.headline: Property, Plant and Equipment (£1,075.25m) and Investment Properties (£96.20m) unable to receive full audit assurance following 2021/22 disclaimer of opinion
findings.detail: The auditors issued a disclaimer of opinion in 2021/22. PPE (net book value £1,075.25 million) and Investment Properties (£96.20 million) are expected to achieve only 'Partial' assurance in 2025/26 because assets within the valuations cycle have not been subject to revaluation and therefore cannot be subject to audit procedures following the prior disclaimers. This assurance gap spans multiple years.
findings.matters: A lender needs audited, reliable asset values to assess security and covenant positions. Inability to obtain full audit assurance on £1.1 billion in property assets four years after a disclaimer indicates persistent control weaknesses or valuation governance failures that could affect financial reporting reliability.
findings.figures: Property, Plant and Equipment: £1,075.25 million net book value; Investment Properties: £96.20 million; Prior disclaimer issued in 2021/22; multiple years without substantial assurance
findings.quote: The maximum assurance level we will be able to report in 2025/26 will be partial, as due to the valuations cycle in place at the Council, there are a number of assets that have not been subject to revaluation in the period that, following previous disclaimers of opinion, have not been subject to audit procedures.

findings.paper_title: Supplementary Agenda Document Pack - Audit committee - 15/09/2026
findings.headline: Lion Homes (Norwich) Ltd subsidiary is in Members' Voluntary Liquidation with unaudited financial statements
findings.detail: The Council's subsidiary company is undergoing a Members' Voluntary Liquidation. The company's 2023/24 financial statements have not been audited and filed, and the 2024/25 financial statements have not yet been prepared. As a result, the company has been consolidated into the Group financial statements on a break-up basis for 2024/25, rather than on a going-concern basis.
findings.matters: A liquidating subsidiary that cannot be audited properly signals either a failed council venture or loss of financial control over group entities. It prevents clean consolidation and audit assurance over group statements for the period covered.
findings.figures: Lion Homes (Norwich) Ltd - a group entity in Members' Voluntary Liquidation; 2023/24 and 2024/25 financial statements not audited/prepared respectively
findings.quote: Lion Homes (Norwich) Ltd is currently undergoing a Members' Voluntary Liquidation process. The Company's financial statements for 2023/24 have not been audited and filed. The 2024/25 financial statements have not yet been prepared. As a result, no subsidiary auditor reporting was prepared for 2024/25. The company has therefore been consolidated into the Group financial statements on a break-up basis.

findings.headline: Council is rebuilding audit assurance after concerns raised in the prior-year audit
findings.detail: The council explicitly states it is working with EY to 'rebuild audit assurance' and has 'sought to address the concerns raised as part of the 2024-25 audit.' This signals that the 2024-25 audit found issues significant enough to require deliberate remediation.
findings.matters: Prior-year audit concerns and the need to rebuild assurance would interest any lender, as they indicate governance or financial control weaknesses discovered by the external auditors.
findings.figures: None provided in this cover page
findings.quote: Council staff have worked constructively with EY throughout the 2025-26 audit and sought to address the concerns raised as part of the 2024-25 audit. The report highlights the progress made to date and we remain committed to work with EY to facilitate the rebuild of audit assurance.

findings.headline: Business continuity risk declining but elevated, with increasing emergency events as key driver
findings.detail: Business continuity risk (CORP06) improved from 16 to 12 this quarter but remains above the risk appetite of 4. The council cites 'increasing instances of events' including 'increased protests and extreme weather instances' as drivers of the likelihood score of 3.
findings.matters: Increasing emergency events and elevated business continuity risk could disrupt council services and affect its ability to meet statutory obligations, impacting lender confidence.
findings.figures: Current score: 12 (down from 16); Risk appetite: 4; Likelihood score: 3
findings.quote: The likelihood score is set at 3 due to the increasing instances of events of this nature at this time with, for example, increased protests and extreme weather instances.

findings.headline: Three-year financial settlement provides greater medium-term funding certainty despite ongoing pressures
findings.detail: The council notes ongoing financial pressures but has received a provisional three-year financial settlement from April 2026 that will support medium-term financial planning. This represents a shift from year-to-year uncertainty to greater medium-term visibility.
findings.matters: A three-year settlement reduces budget uncertainty and supports medium-term financial planning, which is positive for lenders assessing financial stability. However, the council's continued reference to ongoing pressures indicates these remain a concern.
findings.figures: Three-year settlement effective from April 2026
findings.quote: As a result of reforms to local government finance, the council has received a provisional three-year financial settlement, effective from April 2026. This provides greater funding certainty and will support the Council's medium term financial planning

findings.headline: Climate change risks CORP21 and CORP21A escalated to corporate register with current score 20 against risk appetite of 9
findings.detail: Two climate change risks (CORP21 and CORP21A) have been escalated back to the corporate risk register due to new guidance from the UK Climate Change Committee. CORP21 current score is 20 (up from 12 last quarter) against a risk appetite of 9.
findings.matters: A significant reassessment of climate risk exposure (score more than doubled) suggests the council views climate impacts as material to its risk profile and medium-term planning.
findings.figures: CORP21 current score: 20 (up from 12); Risk appetite: 9
findings.quote: The associated risks have been assessed to reflect new UK climate risk guidance from the Climate Change Committee and the scale of the challenge ahead and, as a result, the risk owner has recommended that the risks are added back to the corporate risk register.

findings.headline: Anglia Square demolition delays escalate the risk to corporate level
findings.detail: The Anglia Square risk has been escalated to the corporate risk register due to consistently high current risk score and delays in demolition works. Current risk score is 15 against a risk appetite of 9.
findings.matters: Capital project delays can affect the council's delivery of strategic priorities and may indicate emerging cost or delivery pressures that impact financial standing.
findings.figures: Risk score: 15; Risk appetite: 9
findings.quote: CORP09 Anglia Square –This risk has been escalated from the Major Projects Directorate Risk Register due to the consistently high current risk score and the recommendation from the risk owner that the risk is escalated. The escalation of the risk is mainly due to delays in the demolition works at Anglia square.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - 2025-26 Norwich City Council - LG Risk Reserve Assessment
findings.headline: Audit fees will increase for risk assessment work and potential historical rebuild, with costs not yet agreed.
findings.detail: Activities relating to this risk assessment, the MHCLG submission, and any procedures to rebuild historical assurance fall outside the scale fee agreed in the Audit Planning Report. EY will seek a variation to the fee, but amounts have not been agreed and will be communicated later through formal reporting.
findings.matters: Unquantified additional audit costs add budget pressure to a council already managing disclaimed opinions; the council faces both governance impact and financial cost of addressing audit failure.
findings.figures: Scale fee variation to be sought; amount not yet disclosed
findings.quote: we will seek a variation to the scale fee to reflect these changes to the scope of our work and will communicate further through our reporting once the costs are agreed.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - 2025-26 Norwich City Council - LG Risk Reserve Assessment
findings.headline: Implementation of a new accounting system is heightening audit risk over complex reserves while management capacity is already stretched.
findings.detail: The risk assessment identifies the new accounting system implementation as a factor increasing misstatement risk. This is particularly acute in complex reserves like the Capital Adjustment Account (which involves technical accounting and statutory requirements) because system changes create risk that prior-period errors remain undetected. Management capacity is already constrained by concurrent demands of current-year audit work.
findings.matters: System implementations during periods of audit stress and constrained capacity typically result in control breakdowns and undetected errors. This multiplies the existing audit risk and makes 2025/26 accounts less reliable at the very point assurance should be improving.
findings.figures: Multiple Significant Risk reserves affected by new accounting system; management capacity flagged as limiting factor
findings.quote: the scale and complexity of historic balances requiring reconstruction; the implementation of a new accounting system; insufficient quality or availability of historic supporting evidence; limitations in management capacity to support a historic rebuild alongside the 2025/26 audit

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - 2025-26 Norwich City Council - LG Risk Reserve Assessment
findings.headline: Norwich is falling behind the sector-wide timeline for returning to an unqualified audit opinion and will not have historical gaps addressed in 2025/26.
findings.detail: EY explicitly states the Council's progress falls behind the expected timescales. The NAO guidance expects councils to progress disclaimer → qualified → unqualified, but Norwich will not move forward. EY will not focus audit resources on rebuilding assurance over pre-2023/24 gaps in 2025/26 because Norwich has not demonstrated capacity to complete current-year procedures, and management resources are constrained.
findings.matters: A council unable to complete its own audit and falling behind the sector-wide rebuild timeline signals structural financial reporting and control weaknesses, not temporary stress. This extends the period of unverified accounts and suggests the problems lie in how the council manages its finances and audit process, not circumstances.
findings.figures: Expected 3-to-4-year progression to unqualified per NAO LARRIG; Norwich is explicitly behind
findings.quote: In our view, the Council's progress falls behind the expected timescales set out in LARRIG 01.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - 2025-26 Norwich City Council - LG Risk Reserve Assessment
findings.headline: An uncorrected pension accounting error overstated assets by £35.1 million at March 2024 and remains unaudited.
findings.detail: The Pensions Reserve contains a documented uncorrected prior-year error in which pension assets were overstated and remeasurement losses understated by £35.1 million at 31 March 2024. The error arose from non-application of the IAS 19 asset ceiling requirements. Only partial assurance has been obtained over 2024/25 pension balances, and no assurance has been obtained over the opening balance carrying this error forward.
findings.matters: A £35.1 million unresolved misstatement of pension liabilities remains embedded in the financial position with no audit trail to explain or correct it. This is not a technical point—it is a material hole in reported liabilities.
findings.figures: £35.1 million overstatement of pension assets at 31 March 2024
findings.quote: uncorrected prior-year error relating to the non-application of the IAS 19 asset ceiling requirements under IFRIC 14, which resulted in pension assets being overstated and remeasurement losses being understated by £35.1 million at 31 March 2024.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - 2025-26 Norwich City Council - LG Risk Reserve Assessment
findings.headline: Norwich has received disclaimed audit opinions for two consecutive years and lacks assurance over material reserve balances totalling hundreds of millions.
findings.detail: Norwich received disclaimer opinions in both 2023/24 and 2024/25, meaning auditors could not form any opinion on the financial statements. Planned audit procedures could not be completed in either year. Six major reserves—General Fund Balance, Housing Revenue Account, Capital Receipts Reserve, Capital Grants Unapplied, Capital Adjustment Account, and Revaluation Reserve—are each assessed as "Significant Risk" because audit procedures were not performed in 2021/22 and 2022/23, and procedures remain incomplete in later years.
findings.matters: The inability to obtain an independent audit opinion over core reserve balances is a fundamental breach of financial reporting: lenders cannot verify the council's true financial position, and the finance director cannot be assured their working papers are reliable.
findings.figures: Two consecutive years of disclaimed opinions; six material reserves at Significant Risk
findings.quote: planned procedures could not be completed in either 2023/24 or 2024/25. Therefore, while the "natural" rebuild process has commenced, it has not yet significantly rebuilt assurance.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - EY - Norwich City Council Accompanying Pack
findings.headline: Norwich's audit has a significant weakness in statutory financial reporting arrangements and is behind national recovery timescales.
findings.detail: EY identified a value for money significant weakness in the council's arrangements for statutory financial reporting. Audit procedures for 2023/24 and 2024/25 were limited, leaving gaps in assurance over material balance sheet areas. The council's progress does not meet the expected recovery schedule (LARRIG 01), and the audit opinion likely remains qualified or disclaimed rather than unqualified.
findings.matters: A qualified or disclaimed audit opinion means auditors could not verify material balances on the financial statements. A VFM weakness in financial reporting governance signals control deficiencies in the core finance function that affect the reliability of the position presented to lenders and members.
findings.figures: Limited procedures 2023/24 and 2024/25; off LARRIG 01 recovery schedule
findings.quote: The Council's progress is behind the expected timescales for rebuilding assurance set out in LARRIG 01. This is because limited procedures were completed for 2023/24 and 2024/25 because of the challenges set out earlier in this report, and as referenced in our value for money significant weakness on the Council's arrangements for statutory financial reporting.

findings.paper_title: Progress Report on Internal Audit Activity
findings.headline: Treasury Management audit received Substantial assurance with only minor control gaps identified
findings.detail: The Treasury Management audit completed during 2026/27 confirmed robust governance, effective cashflow management, appropriate segregation of duties, and compliance with regulations. The audit identified only minor improvement opportunities: some active user profiles on Barclays.net for officers no longer in post, and occasional missing investment counterparty documentation.
findings.matters: Lenders assess treasury and investment controls as core to financial stability. Substantial assurance on treasury management, with only housekeeping issues, indicates the council's borrowing and investment framework is operating as designed.
findings.figures: 0 Urgent, 1 Important, 1 Routine recommendations from Treasury Management audit
findings.quote: There is a robust system of internal controls operating effectively to ensure that risks are managed, and process objectives achieved.

findings.paper_title: Progress Report on Internal Audit Activity
findings.headline: Planned Housing Maintenance approval process not being followed for contractor valuations before payment
