findings.headline: General Fund capital expenditure planned to fall from £48.2m in 2025/26 to £8.1m in 2027/28, shifting to revenue contributions of £21m-£25m annually from 2028/29
findings.detail: Capital expenditure plans for the General Fund drop sharply: £48.2m (2025-26) → £21.4m (2026-27) → £8.1m (2027-28). From 2028-29 onwards, the council plans to fund capital through revenue contributions of £21m-£25m annually, indicating shift away from capital investment.
findings.matters: A sharp reduction in capital investment signals either completion of major projects or financial constraint. Revenue contribution to capital is typically a sign of asset underinvestment.

findings.headline: £150m of council debt maturing in three consecutive years with strategy to delay refinancing
findings.detail: Large tranches of PWLB debt mature: £53.2m in 2025-26, £57.5m in 2026-27, and £52.5m in 2027-28. The council's stated strategy is to 'wait as long as possible to refinance due to interest rates', betting on rates falling before these deadlines.
findings.matters: A council postponing refinancing of large debt tranches is exposed if rates don't fall as forecast, and creates lumpy near-term refinancing requirements.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Norwich City Council, Audit Results Report Year ended 31 March 2025
findings.headline: Six internal control deficiencies identified, including one rated as high priority requiring immediate action.
findings.detail: A high-rated deficiency concerns debtor and creditor listings not meeting audit requirements, with unclear responsibility for data cleansing and multiple redirections when EY sought to identify owners. Five additional moderate-rated deficiencies were identified covering delays in HRA expense listings, PPE disclosure errors, NDR appeals provision errors, IFRS 16 disclosure defects, and revenue grant income recognition timing issues.
findings.matters: Control deficiencies of this number and severity indicate systemic weaknesses in financial processes. The high-rated item requires immediate remediation and suggests the finance function lacks clarity on responsibilities and system capabilities.
findings.figures: 1 high-rated, 5 moderate-rated control deficiencies
findings.quote: During our testing of Revenue Grants Received in Advance, we identified an instance where income had been recognised prior to the Council actually receiving the funds.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Norwich City Council, Audit Results Report Year ended 31 March 2025
findings.headline: Management-imposed audit scope limitation: insufficient evidence for creditors and debtors.
findings.detail: During 2024/25, management prioritised work only on account balances where sufficient evidence could be obtained and acknowledged that adequate audit evidence could not be provided for creditors and debtors. These listings included significant opening and gross balances rather than the auditable format requested. Finance staff did not understand the Unit4 ERP system functionality to generate the required listings. This represents a deliberate limitation of the audit scope by management.
findings.matters: Inability to audit major balance sheet items (creditors and debtors) means the council cannot provide assurance on a significant portion of its current liabilities and receivables, key metrics for assessing financial health.
findings.figures: None specific amounts disclosed
findings.quote: During the 2024/25 audit, management prioritised work on account balances where sufficient evidence could be obtained and acknowledged that adequate audit evidence could not be provided for certain areas — specifically creditors and debtors.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Norwich City Council, Audit Results Report Year ended 31 March 2025
findings.headline: Significant VFM weakness: inadequate financial reporting processes and systems.
findings.detail: The council does not have effective processes and systems to support statutory financial reporting. Key working papers were not provided in accordance with agreed timetables or suitable formats. Specifically, creditors and debtors working papers were incomplete, property valuations lacked sufficient supporting evidence, and the NDR appeals provision had errors due to a new team member's lack of familiarity with the process. Management acknowledges further work is required in these areas.
findings.matters: Weak financial reporting systems make it difficult for auditors to obtain necessary evidence and increase the risk of undetected errors in the financial statements. This undermines the reliability of the council's financial data.
findings.figures: None specific
findings.quote: we have also identified a further weakness relating to the Council's arrangements for effective processes and systems to support statutory financial reporting requirements

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Norwich City Council, Audit Results Report Year ended 31 March 2025
findings.headline: Significant VFM weakness: inadequate governance of subsidiaries and partnerships.
findings.detail: The council had no documented policies, procedures or governance oversight of its subsidiaries. The articles of association for Lion Homes did not require proper interaction with the council. Neither the Board of Directors nor the Shareholder Panel had terms of reference ensuring mandatory reporting to the council. The subsidiary operated independently with no requirement to report issues, resulting in financial problems not being identified in a timely manner and preventing effective intervention. This lack of structure significantly contributed to the challenges at the subsidiary.
findings.matters: Weak subsidiary governance put the council at financial risk and exposed taxpayers to uncontrolled company losses. It indicates the council cannot safely manage additional investments or companies.
findings.figures: None specific
findings.quote: The Council did not have in place adequate policies, procedures or governance oversight of its part, or wholly, owned companies. This lack of oversight resulted in Council Members and Officers being unaware of inappropriate operating procedures and challenges at one of its subsidiaries.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Norwich City Council, Audit Results Report Year ended 31 March 2025
findings.headline: Statutory deadline for publishing audited financial statements missed by nearly three months.
findings.detail: The financial statements were required to be published by 30 June 2025 under the Accounts and Audit Regulations, but were not published until 26 September 2025 (88 days late). This was due to delays in finalising group financial statements, largely stemming from the Lion Homes subsidiary issues. A Notice of Delay was issued. The audit itself cannot be finalised before the statutory backstop date of 27 February 2026 due to the deferred Audit Committee approval.
findings.matters: Missing statutory reporting deadlines indicates poor financial controls and is itself a regulatory breach. Delays in accounts publication delay audit completion and extend uncertainty about the council's true financial position.
findings.figures: Deadline 30 June 2025, actual publication 26 September 2025
findings.quote: The financial statements were not published by the 30 June 2025 deadline set out in the Accounts and Audit Regulations. This was due to delays in finalising the group financial statements. The required Notice of Delay was issued and the financial statements were subsequently published on 26 September 2025.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Norwich City Council, Audit Results Report Year ended 31 March 2025
findings.headline: Prior-period pension liability overstated by £35.1 million due to asset ceiling calculation error.
findings.detail: Management did not apply the required asset ceiling adjustment to the pension asset in 2023/24. The auditors identified that the defined benefit pension liability was overstated by £35.1 million. This material misstatement was not corrected in the 2024/25 financial statements per management's choice, meaning it remains in the accounts.
findings.matters: A £35.1m overstatement of pension liabilities materially misstates the council's financial position and net assets. This affects the balance sheet that lenders rely on for credit assessment.
findings.figures: £35.1 million
findings.quote: management obtained an updated asset ceiling report from the actuary highlighting that the defined pension liability is overstated by £35.1 million

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Norwich City Council, Audit Results Report Year ended 31 March 2025
findings.headline: Wholly-owned housing subsidiary Lion Homes is entering member voluntary liquidation with uncertain loan recoverability.
findings.detail: The council has significant long-term debtor balances from loans to Lion Homes Ltd, now at risk of not being recoverable. Material errors were identified in the subsidiary's 2023/24 financial information, requiring a prior period adjustment in the 2024/25 statements. The council had no adequate governance arrangements to monitor the subsidiary, leaving members and officers unaware of operating problems until too late. The subsidiary operated independently with no mandatory reporting requirement to the council, preventing timely identification of financial issues.
findings.matters: Loss of a wholly-owned trading company represents a direct capital loss to the council. The loans may not be recovered. This reflects poor governance and exposes whether the council can safely operate subsidiary companies.
findings.figures: Long-term debtor balances from loans to subsidiary (amount not quantified in this section)
findings.quote: A financial sustainability risk has been identified concerning the council's wholly owned subsidiary, Lion Homes Ltd. The Council has significant long term debtor balances, arising from loans issued to the subsidiary. There is a risk that some of these balances may not be recoverable.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Norwich City Council, Audit Results Report Year ended 31 March 2025
findings.headline: 2024/25 financial statements will receive a disclaimed audit opinion, meaning the council's accounts cannot be relied upon.
findings.detail: The auditors cannot conclude that the 2024/25 financial statements are free from material and pervasive misstatement. This follows a disclaimed opinion in 2023/24. The auditors were unable to complete planned procedures for key audit areas including management override risks, capitalisation of expenditure, and property valuations. The lack of assurance over opening balances from the prior year disclaimer compounds the inability to assure current year movements and closing balances.
findings.matters: A disclaimed audit opinion means the council's financial statements cannot be relied upon for lending decisions or financial planning. This is the highest level of audit concern short of discovering fraud.
findings.figures: None specific, but covers all material account balances
findings.quote: We therefore anticipate issuing a disclaimed 2024/25 audit opinion.

news_drafts.headline: Norwich reports provisional £0.543m General Fund underspend and £4.391m housing surplus for 2025-26
news_drafts.lead:
Norwich City Council ended 2025-26 with a provisional underspend of £0.543m on its General Fund revenue account, which covers day-to-day spending outside council housing. The figure appears in the council's Annual Governance Statement, in which the council reports on itself, at Appendix D of the papers for the audit committee meeting of 10 November 2026.

The statement says the underspend went on to contribute to reserves. The figures are provisional outturn, the position before the accounts are finalised.

The same statement reports a surplus of £4.391m on the housing revenue account, the ring-fenced account for the council's own housing, paid for by rents. The council says that surplus "will be utilised in future budget planning".

news_drafts.headline: Norwich repaid £53.2m debt with no new borrowing as capital spending fell 40% short
news_drafts.lead: Norwich council repaid £53.2m of Public Works Loan Board debt in 2025-26 and took zero new external borrowing, while maintaining £68.5m in cash reserves. The council early-repaid a £5m Barclays loan in July 2025 and received a £554,000 discount from the lender. However, the council spent only £56.5m of its £94.8m capital budget, underspending by £38.3m. General Fund capital was £23m underspent and housing revenue account capital £16m underspent. This lower spending also reduced borrowing needs to £4.7m against a budgeted £7.5m. Officers are deferring new borrowing pending lower interest rates, despite a capital financing requirement of £314m — the total the council has spent on long-lived assets it has not yet paid for — and £7.5m of maturing debt due in 2026-27. The council also faced an unexpected financing cost pressure: general fund financing costs reached 7.54% of net revenue against a 0.97% forecast, mainly because of unbudgeted impacts from new lease accounting rules and changes to minimum revenue provision policy.
